title: multiplication and division of two- or three-digit numbers by one-digit numbers

lesson.title: Big Numbers, One Little Number: Multiplying and Dividing Made Easy

steps.say: Hi friend, it's Ms. Yuanyuan! Imagine you and your family go to the farmers market in Vancouver. Blueberries cost four dollars a basket, and you want to buy twenty-three baskets for a big family party. You could add four plus four plus four twenty-three times... but oh my, that would take forever! This is exactly why we have multiplication. Multiplication is just a fast way to add the same number over and over.

visual.caption: Six baskets with four dollars each — imagine seventeen more!

steps.say: Here is the big secret. When a number is too big to hold in your head, we break it into friendly pieces. Twenty-three is really twenty plus three. So twenty-three times four becomes twenty times four, plus three times four. Breaking a number into pieces is called decomposing, and it is your superpower.

Let's draw it as a rectangle, like a garden bed. The long side is twenty-three and the short side is four. See how the rectangle splits into a big chunk and a small chunk? The big chunk is twenty times four, which is eighty. The small chunk is three times four, which is twelve. Now add them: eighty plus twelve is ninety-two. So twenty-three baskets of blueberries cost ninety-two dollars!

Now let's try a three-digit number. Your class is collecting bottles for a fundraiser and each of the one hundred forty-two students brings three bottles. Break one hundred forty-two into one hundred, forty, and two. One hundred times three is three hundred. Forty times three is one hundred twenty. Two times three is six. Add them up: three hundred plus one hundred twenty is four hundred twenty, plus six is four hundred twenty-six bottles.

visual.caption: 142 = one hundred + four tens + two ones

steps.say: Now here is the lovely part. Division is just multiplication walking backwards. If ninety-two dollars bought us four-dollar baskets, then ninety-two divided by four tells us how many baskets we got. And we already know the answer is twenty-three! Every multiplication fact gives you a division fact for free. They are best friends.

Let's do a real sharing problem. You baked seventy-five granola bars and you want to share them equally among five friends at recess. Break seventy-five into fifty plus twenty-five. Fifty divided by five is ten. Twenty-five divided by five is five. Ten plus five is fifteen. Each friend gets fifteen granola bars. Let's check by multiplying backwards: fifteen times five is seventy-five. It works!

visual.caption: 75 granola bars shared into 5 equal groups of 15

steps.say: Sometimes things don't share out perfectly, and that is totally okay. Say you have thirty-eight stickers to share among four kids. Four times nine is thirty-six, which is as close as we can get without going over. Thirty-eight take away thirty-six leaves two. So each kid gets nine stickers and two stickers are left over. We call that leftover part the remainder.

visual.caption: 4 groups of 9, with 2 stickers left over

steps.say: So remember, my friend: big numbers are not scary, they are just small numbers hiding together. Break them apart, work with the friendly pieces, then put them back together. And if you ever forget a division answer, just ask yourself, what times this gives me that?

lesson.answer: Break the big number into friendly place-value pieces, work each piece, then put them back together — and remember, division is just multiplication walking backwards.

practice.question: A rope at the community centre in Kelowna is 156 centimetres long. Ms. Yuanyuan cuts it into 4 equal skipping ropes. How long is each skipping rope? (Hint: break 156 into 120 plus 36.)
practice.answer: 39 centimetres. Because 120 divided by 4 is 30, and 36 divided by 4 is 9, so 30 plus 9 equals 39. Check: 39 times 4 equals 156. ✓
